algorithm.title: Overall Approach to Patient with Suspected T1DM.

cell.label: Suspect T1DM due to abrupt onset polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss. Fasting glucose ≥126, casual glucose ≥200 mg/dL, or abnormal glucose tolerance test?
Repeat testing on another day. Abnormal?
Monitor patient, repeat testing if symptomatic.
Same day referral for care and education. Diagnosis of T1DM clear?
Type 1 diabetes. Treat with intensive insulin therapy (multiple daily injections or continuous insulin infusion). Optimize cardiovascular risk factors. A1C at goal for age?
Consider postprandial hyperglycemia (pramlintide may be helpful), adherence, depression, and eating disorders.
Keep at least quarterly follow-up during medication changes.
Check diabetes autoantibodies (GAD65) and basal and/or stimulated C-peptide. Positive GAD65 and low C-peptide?
Highly suggestive of T2DM. Treat as appropriate.
T1DM patient needs surgery. Schedule as first case in morning if possible.
1-2 wk prior to surgery, assess glycemic management? Is it adequate for age?
Preoperative management based on regimen.
Expected duration of surgery >2 h?
Continue pump.
Start glucose-insulin infusion for surgery.

Hold breakfast, check morning glucose. If the blood glucose level is >250, use the insulin correction factor to calculate the necessary insulin dose for correction to 100-200 range. Insulin correction factor: take 1500 and divide by patient's total daily insulin requirement. That is the amount 1 unit of insulin will decrease the blood glucose level. For example, if a patient's total daily dose of insulin is 50 units, it takes 1 unit of insulin to decrease her surgar by 30 mg/dL.
Day of surgery: No short-acting insulin. Give any basal insulin as scheduled.
Day of surgery: No short-acting insulin. Only ½ dose of NPH.
Adjust regimen prior to clearance.
If possible delay surgery until pH, electrolytes, and glucose is stabilized … then preoperative management based on regimen.
